about:
A dream rarely fits in one box. The same dream can be lucid, joyful and recurring at once: lucid describes how aware you were, joyful describes the feeling, and recurring describes how it returns over time. That is why the types sit in four groups (consciousness level, emotional content, narrative pattern and special significance), and why one dream can carry types from several groups together.

When you save a dream, you can tick the types that fit under Dream Categories in Add details. When you ask for an analysis, DREAM CODE also suggests the types it recognises, the main one first, with a sentence on why each fits. Your own choices always stay: the suggestions are a second opinion, and you are the one who was there.

groups.name: Consciousness Level
groups.about: How aware you were while you were dreaming. Most dreams unfold without any sense that they are dreams; sometimes awareness flickers or fully switches on, and sometimes the dream happens right at the edge of sleep. These types describe the state of mind you dreamed in, not what the dream was about.

groups.name: Emotional Content
groups.about: The feeling that ran through the dream and stayed with you afterwards. Many dream researchers place emotion at the core of dreaming, and the book behind DREAM CODE goes further: the feeling comes first, the images follow. These types name the emotional tone that coloured the dream most strongly.

groups.name: Narrative Pattern
groups.about: How the dream is shaped as a story, and how it connects with your other dreams. Some dreams repeat, some continue from night to night, some break into fragments, some sweep you across whole worlds, and some look like an ordinary Tuesday. These types often become clearest when you look back over your journal.

groups.name: Special Significance
groups.about: Dreams that feel as if they mean something beyond the night itself: dreams that seem to anticipate, heal, solve, reunite or touch something larger than you. People in every culture and era have given dreams like these special weight. These types describe how a dream felt and what it did for you; they make no claim about what lies beyond the dream.

types.name: Normal Dream
types.short: An ordinary dream from regular sleep, lived from inside the story without knowing you are dreaming.
types.description:
Most dreams are normal dreams in this sense: you are inside the story, and it never occurs to you that it is a dream. Rooms change, people appear and vanish, time folds, and you accept all of it, because the part of the mind that would normally ask whether this makes sense has gone quiet. Only on waking do you notice how strange, or how ordinary, it all was.

Normal dreams happen throughout the night. They are most vivid in REM sleep, which returns roughly every ninety minutes and lengthens toward morning, but they also occur in the other stages of sleep, where they tend to be shorter and more like drifting thoughts. Most are forgotten within minutes of waking unless you catch them.

Being normal does not make a dream unimportant. This is the everyday working dream: the one that mixes yesterday's worries with old memories, rehearses social situations and replays feelings you did not have time to finish. Many other types in this dictionary describe what a dream contained or how it felt; this one describes the state of mind you dreamed it in.
signs: You only realised it was a dream after you woke up.
Impossible things felt perfectly natural at the time.
The story moved from scene to scene without you questioning it.
You remember it in pieces that grow fainter as the morning goes on.
types.may_reflect: Normal dreams often reflect what has been on your mind: the people, worries, hopes and unfinished feelings of recent days, woven together with older memories that share the same emotional colour. A useful starting question is not what the images mean in general, but what feeling ran through the dream and where you have met that feeling lately.
practices: Keep this journal or a notebook by the bed and record the dream before you check your phone; even a few words help you remember.
Lie still for a moment on waking and replay the dream backwards from the last scene you can recall.
Note the main feeling first, then the images, then any link to the day before.
After a couple of weeks, read your entries together and look for the people, places and feelings that keep returning.
types.science: Laboratory dream research took off when Aserinsky and Kleitman (1953) described rapid eye movement (REM) sleep and found that people woken from it usually reported dreaming. Foulkes (1962) then showed that dreaming also happens outside REM sleep, though those reports are often shorter. Hall and Van de Castle (1966) created a system for coding dream content and published norms showing that typical dreams feature familiar people and settings, with more misfortune and negative emotion than good fortune and joy. Domhoff (2003) reviewed this work in support of the continuity hypothesis: dreams largely carry on the concerns and relationships of waking life. Why we dream is still debated, from Hobson and McCarley's (1977) activation-synthesis model to theories that see dreaming as emotional and memory processing.

lenses.freud: Freud called the interpretation of dreams the royal road to the unconscious. A Freudian reading would separate the manifest dream, the story you remember, from the latent thoughts behind it, and look for a wish expressed in disguise, often built from day residue, the small impressions of the previous day. His method was free association: letting each image lead to whatever comes to mind.
lenses.jung: Jung saw ordinary dreams as the psyche's natural way of keeping itself in balance. A Jungian reading would ask what the dream compensates for: which attitude, feeling or part of you is missing from your waking view. On the subjective level, every person and place in the dream can be read as an aspect of yourself.
lenses.hvdc: This is the kind of dream the coding system was built for. It counts who appears (known people or strangers, men or women, animals), how they interact, what goes well and what goes badly, the emotions, and the settings. In the published norms, typical dreams take place in familiar settings with known people and contain more misfortune and negative emotion than good fortune and happiness, which is normal rather than a warning sign.
lenses.modern: Modern research treats ordinary dreaming as the brain's offline work: weaving recent experience into older memory, processing emotion while stress chemistry is low during REM sleep, and simulating social and threatening situations. Predictive processing accounts add that the dreaming brain keeps generating its model of the world without input from the senses, which is why dreams feel real from the inside.

types.name: Lucid Dream
types.short: A dream in which you know you are dreaming while it is still happening, and can sometimes steer it.
types.description:
In a lucid dream a realisation arrives from inside the dream: this is a dream. Sometimes it comes from noticing something impossible, a clock that never reads the same twice or a light switch that does nothing; sometimes it simply dawns on you. The dream usually carries on, but now you are watching it, and often taking part in it, with your waking judgement switched back on.

Lucidity comes in degrees. Some people only notice and then wake up; others can stay, look around, change direction, fly, call up a person or a place, or ask the dream a question. Control is never complete, and the dream often answers back in surprising ways. Excitement is the most common reason a lucid dream ends early, which is why experienced lucid dreamers learn to stay calm and steady inside the dream.

Many people have had at least one lucid dream, often in childhood or the teenage years, and a smaller group have them regularly. It is also a skill that can be learned, at least in part. People use it for adventure, for creative work, for rehearsing skills, and for facing frightening figures in recurring nightmares from a position of safety.
signs: You thought or said “this is a dream” while the dream was still going on.
You tested the dream, for example by looking at your hands, reading something twice or trying to push a finger through your palm.
You chose what to do next, such as flying, changing the scene or speaking to a dream character.
Colours, sensations or your sense of being there felt unusually vivid once you knew.
You woke soon after realising, often from excitement.
types.may_reflect: Lucid dreams may reflect a mind that is practising awareness: people who meditate, play immersive video games or keep a dream journal often report more of them. They can also come in periods of curiosity and growth, when you are learning to notice your own patterns. What you choose to do once you are lucid, whether to explore, confront, create or simply look, can say as much about you as the dream itself.
practices: Write in your dream journal every morning; better dream recall is the foundation of every lucid dreaming method.
Do reality checks during the day: read a line of text, look away, read it again, and genuinely ask yourself whether you are dreaming.

As you fall asleep, go back over a recent dream, imagine noticing the moment it turned strange, and repeat an intention such as “next time I am dreaming, I will notice” (this is the core of LaBerge's mnemonic induction method).
Once you are lucid, slow down: rub your hands together, touch something solid or look at the ground to steady the dream before trying anything ambitious.
Decide in advance what you want to try, so the moment is not wasted; a simple goal, such as asking a dream figure what it stands for, works well.
types.science: The term was introduced by the Dutch psychiatrist Frederik van Eeden in 1913, and the Marquis d'Hervey de Saint-Denys had already described guiding his own dreams in 1867. Laboratory confirmation came when lucid dreamers made agreed eye movements while recordings showed they were in REM sleep, first in Keith Hearne's work in England and then in Stephen LaBerge's at Stanford, which LaBerge described in Lucid Dreaming (1985). Voss and colleagues (2009) found more activity in frontal brain regions during lucid dreams, especially in the gamma frequency range, than during ordinary REM dreams: a pattern somewhere between dreaming and waking. A review of induction methods by Stumbrys and colleagues (2012) found some techniques promising but none reliable for everyone, with the evidence still limited. Konkoly and colleagues (2021) went further and held simple two-way exchanges with dreamers during lucid REM sleep.

lenses.freud: In later editions of The Interpretation of Dreams, Freud acknowledged that some people know they are dreaming and can direct their dreams, citing Hervey de Saint-Denys. A Freudian reading would be curious about what you chose to do once you had control: a lucid dream lets wishes act more openly, so the choices themselves become material for free association.
lenses.jung: Jung did not make lucid dreaming a focus of his work, but his method of active imagination, a waking dialogue with images from the unconscious, is close to it in spirit. A Jungian reading would treat the lucid dream as a meeting between the conscious self and the unconscious, and would suggest asking dream figures who they are rather than commanding them, because the unconscious has an intelligence of its own.
lenses.hvdc: The coding system was not designed to record awareness, so lucidity itself is not coded. What it would pick up are the consequences: successes achieved by the dreamer, flying and other unusual activities, and deliberate interactions with dream characters. Comparing your lucid and non-lucid dreams on these points can be revealing.
lenses.modern: Lucid dreaming is studied as a hybrid state: REM sleep with some of waking self-reflection restored, linked to greater activity in frontal regions of the brain. Researchers use it as a tool, because a lucid dreamer can signal from inside the dream, and people use it as a skill for rehearsal, creativity and, in some therapy research, for changing the course of recurring nightmares.

types.caution: Methods that wake you during the night can cost you sleep. If practising leaves you tired, or blurs the line between dreaming and waking in a way that unsettles you, take a break; if that feeling persists, talk to a doctor.

types.name: Semi-Lucid Dream
types.short: A dream with partial or flickering awareness: you sense something is off, or know for a moment, without fully taking hold.
types.description:
Semi-lucid dreams sit between ordinary dreaming and full lucidity. You might feel that something is not quite right, wonder for a moment whether this could be a dream, and then let the thought slip away. You might know you are dreaming yet still follow the plot as if bound by it, or become lucid for a few seconds before the story carries you back in.

Many people recognise these states once they have a name for them: the dream where you thought “this is like a dream” without drawing the conclusion; the one where you knew you could fly but felt you should not; the false awakening, in which you wake up, get dressed and start your morning, only to wake again for real. The researcher Celia Green called the questioning moment before lucidity a pre-lucid dream.

Semi-lucid dreams are worth recording because they show awareness already stirring. For anyone interested in lucid dreaming they are the doorway; for everyone else they are a fascinating glimpse of the sleeping mind partly watching itself.
signs: You wondered whether you might be dreaming, but did not check, or decided you were awake.
You knew it was a dream but still felt bound by its rules or its plot.
Awareness came and went, and you slipped back into the story.
You had a false awakening: you dreamed you woke up in your own room.
Something odd caught your attention, such as writing that changed or a clock that made no sense.
types.may_reflect: Partial awareness may reflect a mind that is becoming more attentive to its own experience, often when you have started paying closer attention to your dreams, are sleeping in later, or are going through a reflective period. The moments where you almost noticed can also mirror waking life: places where you sense something is off but have not yet put it into words.
practices: In your journal, mark the exact moment you almost realised; these dream signs often repeat and can become your cue for full lucidity.
Make a habit of doing a reality check whenever something surprises you during the day, so the habit carries into your dreams.
If false awakenings are a pattern for you, check something simple each time you wake, such as whether a light switch works or whether writing stays the same when you read it twice.
When awareness flickers in a dream, try a calm action that steadies it, such as looking at your hands or touching a wall.
types.science: Researchers increasingly treat lucidity as a set of separate abilities rather than an on and off switch. Voss and colleagues (2013) developed a questionnaire that measures distinct aspects of dream awareness, such as insight that one is dreaming, control, memory of waking life and a sense of detachment, and it shows that many dreams contain some of these features without all of them. Celia Green's book Lucid Dreams (1968) described pre-lucid dreams and false awakenings in detail. The reality checks and intention methods reviewed by Stumbrys and colleagues (2012) are, in effect, ways of turning these half-noticed moments into full recognition.

lenses.freud: Freud observed that dreamers sometimes think “it is only a dream” in the middle of a dream, and read this as the mind lowering the importance of what it is being shown, so that sleep can continue. A Freudian reading of a semi-lucid dream would ask which part of the dream prompted that half-dismissal, and what it might be guarding.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading would see the flicker of awareness as consciousness reaching toward the unconscious without yet meeting it fully. The figures and images present at that moment deserve particular attention, because they mark the threshold where the conscious self is beginning to take part.
lenses.hvdc: The coding system's confusion category, which covers surprise, puzzlement and uncertainty, is often where semi-lucid moments appear. Otherwise the dream is coded like any other, so a false awakening would usually show up as a familiar indoor setting, typically the bedroom.
lenses.modern: Semi-lucid states fit the modern view that consciousness during sleep is graded, with self-reflection partly restored in some REM periods. False awakenings are thought to arise when the brain builds a convincing model of a familiar morning routine; they are common and harmless, although occasionally unsettling.

types.name: Hypnagogic/Hypnopompic
types.short: Images, sounds and sensations at the edge of sleep, as you drift off (hypnagogic) or as you wake (hypnopompic).
types.description:
At the edges of sleep the mind puts on its own brief show. As you drift off you may see shifting patterns, faces, landscapes or scenes from your day, hear your name or a snatch of music, or feel as though you are falling or floating. On waking, an image can linger for a moment over the real room. The first kind are called hypnagogic, the second hypnopompic, and both are a normal part of how the brain moves between waking and sleep.

Two transition experiences are especially common. A hypnic jerk is the sudden full-body twitch as you start to fall asleep, often with a feeling of falling; most people have one at some point. Sleep paralysis is waking up, or nearly falling asleep, unable to move for a few seconds or a minute, because the muscle relaxation of REM sleep is still in place; it can come with a sense of presence, pressure on the chest or vivid images. It can be frightening, but it is usually harmless, and knowing what is happening tends to make it far less alarming.

These border states can also be creative. Inventors and artists, from Thomas Edison to Salvador Dalí, are said to have dozed while holding an object that would drop and wake them just as the images began, to catch ideas from this zone.
signs: It happened as you were falling asleep or just waking up, not in the middle of the night.
The images were brief, shifting or kaleidoscopic, or replayed something you did that day.
You heard a sound or a voice, or felt a sudden jolt or a falling sensation.
You were briefly unable to move, perhaps with a feeling that someone was in the room.
You were not sure whether you were awake or asleep.
types.may_reflect: Sleep-onset images often replay whatever has absorbed you lately, a game, a long drive, a day of work, as the brain begins sorting recent experience. How often they happen can also reflect your sleep: irregular hours, sleep loss, stress and caffeine make transition experiences, including hypnic jerks and sleep paralysis, more likely. They are usually a sign of the brain changing state, not a message about danger.
practices: Keep a notebook within reach and jot down sleep-onset images the moment you notice them; they fade within seconds.
If you experience sleep paralysis, remind yourself that it will pass; breathe slowly and try moving a finger or a toe, which often ends it.
Regular sleep times, less caffeine later in the day and enough total sleep tend to reduce hypnic jerks and episodes of sleep paralysis.
For creative use, hold a question loosely in mind as you drift off and let images come without forcing them; write down whatever appears.
types.science: The French scholar Alfred Maury named the hypnagogic state in the nineteenth century, and Andreas Mavromatis gathered the research and first-person accounts in Hypnagogia (1987). Stickgold and colleagues (2000) found that people who had been playing the game Tetris often saw falling blocks as they fell asleep, even participants with amnesia who could not remember playing, which suggests that sleep-onset imagery draws on recent learning. Lacaux and colleagues (2021) found that people who spent a short time in the lightest stage of sleep were more likely to discover a hidden rule in a problem afterwards. Reviews of sleep paralysis, such as Sharpless and Barber (2011), show that many people experience it at least once, and that it is more likely when sleep is disrupted.

lenses.freud: Freud took a close interest in Herbert Silberer's observations of how, when drowsy, an abstract thought could turn into a picture that symbolised it. A Freudian reading of sleep-onset images would treat them as a rare chance to watch the dream-work begin, translating thoughts into pictures, and would ask which thought each image stands for.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading would see the threshold of sleep as a place where images from the unconscious rise before the conscious self steps away. Jung's method of active imagination works in a similar borderland, holding an image in awareness and letting it move, so hypnagogic images can be a natural starting point for that kind of reflection.
lenses.hvdc: Sleep-onset reports are usually short, with few characters and few interactions, so there is often little for the coding system to count. When sleep paralysis is involved, the coding would note apprehension and, sometimes, an uncertain or imaginary character sensed in the room.
lenses.modern: Researchers describe falling asleep as a gradual, uneven handover, with parts of the brain going offline at different moments, which explains how you can see dream images while still half aware of the room. Sleep paralysis is understood as the muscle relaxation of REM sleep continuing into wakefulness, and the sense of a presence as the brain's threat systems trying to make sense of that unusual state.

types.caution: Hypnic jerks and occasional sleep paralysis are common and usually harmless. If sleep paralysis is frequent or very distressing, or if you also fall asleep suddenly during the day, talk to a doctor; these can be signs of a sleep condition that can be checked and helped.

types.name: Joyful/Euphoric
types.short: A dream full of happiness, delight or euphoria that you may carry with you into the morning.
types.description:
Some dreams are simply wonderful. You fly over a glittering city, laugh until you cry with old friends, dance, fall in love, find a hidden room full of treasures, or feel a lightness that waking life rarely offers. Joyful and euphoric dreams can be gentle and warm or exhilarating and wild, and they often leave a glow that colours the whole of the next day.

Because people tend to remember and retell their troubling dreams, joyful dreams can seem rare. They are not. When dreamers rate their own dream emotions, rather than leaving it to outside judges reading the reports, positive feelings show up far more often than most people expect.

A joyful dream can be a celebration of something real, a taste of a wish not yet fulfilled, or a reminder of capacities you may have forgotten: playfulness, freedom, connection. The book behind DREAM CODE suggests starting with the feeling itself: where in your waking life do you feel this way, or long to?
signs: You woke up smiling, energised or reluctant to leave the dream.
The dream was full of laughter, warmth, love, freedom or wonder.
Things went right: you succeeded, found what you were looking for, or were welcomed.
Colours, music or sensations felt brighter than usual.
types.may_reflect: Joyful dreams may reflect real contentment, relief after a hard stretch, excitement about something new, or a longing for more joy than daily life currently allows. They can also show what nourishes you: the people, places and activities that appear in your happiest dreams are worth noticing while you are awake.
practices: Write the dream down with as much sensory detail as you can, then reread it on a difficult day.
Name the exact feeling (joy, relief, awe, belonging) and note one place in waking life where you could find a little more of it.
If the dream featured someone in particular, consider getting in touch with them or doing something you used to enjoy together.
Return to the dream as a short visualisation before sleep; some people find this invites more pleasant dreams.
types.science: Research using Hall and Van de Castle's (1966) coding found more negative than positive emotion in typical dream reports, which helped create the impression that dreaming is mostly unpleasant. However, Schredl and Doll (1998) showed that when dreamers rate their own dream emotions, positive and negative feelings come out roughly balanced, and that outside judges tend to miss the positive ones. Theories of dream function have often focused on threat (Revonsuo 2000), but the social simulation theory proposed by Revonsuo, Tuominen and Valli (2015) suggests that dreams also rehearse bonding, cooperation and affection.

lenses.freud: For Freud, joyful dreams are the clearest examples of wish fulfilment, close to the simple dreams of young children who dream of the outing or the treat they were denied during the day. A Freudian reading would ask which wish the dream fulfils, and whether a less obvious wish sits behind the happy surface.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading would ask what the joy compensates for. Euphoric dreams can arrive when waking life has become too narrow or too serious, restoring a sense of play, the energy of the child archetype, or a glimpse of the Self as wholeness; they may also point to a potential that is ready to be lived.
lenses.hvdc: The coding would note happiness as the emotion, friendliness in the interactions, and good fortunes and successes in the outcomes. In the published norms these are less frequent than their negative counterparts, so a run of joyful dreams in your journal can stand out clearly against typical dream content.
lenses.modern: Modern views see positive dreams as part of emotional processing too: sleep may help consolidate rewarding experiences as well as soften painful ones. Joyful dreams also fit the continuity hypothesis, carrying waking happiness, hope and close relationships into the night.

types.name: Anxiety/Fear
types.short: A dream charged with worry, pressure or fear, such as being late, unprepared, lost or exposed.
types.description:
Anxiety dreams are the dreams of everyday worry. You are late and the bus never comes; you sit an exam for a course you forgot you were taking; your phone will not dial; your teeth crumble; you cannot find the right room; you realise you are not wearing enough clothes. The fear is real but usually not overwhelming, more a steady pressure than terror, and the dream often ends without being resolved.

These themes are remarkably widespread. Surveys of typical dreams find that being chased, falling, school and exam scenes, being late and losing teeth turn up across very different countries and generations. They tend to cluster around times of change, responsibility or evaluation: a new job, a move, a deadline, a relationship at a turning point.

An anxiety dream is not a forecast that things will go wrong. It is closer to a rehearsal, the mind running through what it fears so that the feeling can be met and, often, softened. Looking at what the dream is worried about, rather than its literal plot, usually points to the waking source.
signs: You felt worried, rushed, embarrassed or under pressure for much of the dream.
Things kept going wrong: missed transport, a test you could not answer, a task you could not finish.
You woke with a racing heart or a lingering unease, but not terror.
The dream echoed a current stress, even if the setting was different.
types.may_reflect: Anxiety dreams may reflect a feeling of being judged, unprepared or out of control somewhere in your life, or a change that asks more of you than feels comfortable. They often appear before important events and fade once the pressure has passed. They can also point to worries you have been too busy to feel during the day.
practices: Write down in one sentence what was at stake in the dream (for example, “I was not ready and everyone could see”), then ask where you feel that now.
Spend a few minutes before bed writing down tomorrow's worries and one next step for each, so your mind has less to carry into sleep.
Rewrite the ending while awake: imagine the bus arriving or the exam questions making sense, and notice how your body responds.
Use a short wind-down routine, such as slow breathing, a warm shower or a few pages of a calm book, to settle before sleep.
types.science: Nielsen and colleagues (2003), surveying university students, found that typical themes such as being chased, falling, school and exams were reported by a large share of people. Revonsuo's (2000) threat simulation theory proposes that dreaming rehearses threatening situations so that responses to them improve, and Domhoff's (2003) continuity hypothesis predicts that waking worries will appear in dreams. Arnulf and colleagues (2014) found that medical students who dreamed about an important entrance exam on the night before it, often with stressful content, tended to do better on it, which fits the idea that anxious dreams can be preparation rather than omen. Walker and van der Helm (2009) proposed that REM sleep helps take the sting out of emotional memories.

lenses.freud: Freud noticed that people often dream of failing exams they actually passed long ago, and read this as a kind of reassurance: you were afraid before, and you managed. More generally, he saw anxiety in dreams as a sign that a disguised wish or impulse had come too close to the surface. A Freudian reading would look for what the anxiety is protecting you from noticing.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading would ask what the anxiety compensates for. If waking life is all confidence and control, a dream of being unprepared may balance an inflated persona; if waking life is overwhelming, the dream may be showing the strain honestly. These scenes often show the persona, the face we present to others, starting to slip.
lenses.hvdc: The coding would note apprehension as the main emotion, failures by the dreamer, misfortunes such as losing things or missing transport, and often familiar settings such as school or work. Apprehension is among the most frequently coded emotions in the published norms, so anxious dreams are typical rather than exceptional.
lenses.modern: Modern research sees anxiety dreams as the night side of daytime worry. Threat simulation theory suggests they rehearse coping, and emotional processing models suggest that dreaming through a worry in the low-stress chemistry of REM sleep can reduce its charge. When stress is high, sleep becomes lighter and more broken, so more of these dreams are remembered.

types.caution: Occasional anxiety dreams are a normal part of life. If anxious dreams come most nights for weeks, disturb your sleep, or you feel anxious through much of the day, talk to a doctor or therapist; support can make a real difference.

types.name: Nightmare
types.short: A frightening or deeply upsetting dream that often wakes you up.
types.description:
A nightmare is a dream frightening or distressing enough that it often wakes you, usually with a racing heart and a vivid memory of what happened. Being chased or attacked, falling, losing someone, being trapped, facing a monster or an intruder: the content varies, but the feeling is fear, horror, grief, anger or disgust at full strength. Nightmares mostly come from REM sleep, so they are more common in the second half of the night.

Nearly everyone has nightmares from time to time. They are most common in childhood, and in adults they tend to increase with stress, illness, grief, changes in medication, poor sleep, or after frightening experiences. A nightmare is your mind dealing with something hard. It is not a sign that something is wrong with you, and it is not a prediction of what will happen.

Nightmares also respond well to attention. Writing them down, talking about them and, especially, imagining a new ending while awake can make them less frequent and less intense. When nightmares follow a frightening event, they often soften gradually as the experience is processed.
signs: The dream woke you up, or you woke very frightened, sad or upset.
You remember it vividly, often with a sense of threat or danger.
Your heart was racing or you felt shaky when you woke.
You felt reluctant to go back to sleep in case it continued.
types.may_reflect: Nightmares may reflect stress, fear or pain that has been building up, a recent shock, or an old experience that something in the present has stirred. Their images are often exaggerated and symbolic: a monster may stand for a feeling, a situation or a part of life that feels too big to face. What frightened you most in the dream (being trapped, being hurt, losing someone, feeling powerless) is often the most useful clue.
practices: When you wake from a nightmare, ground yourself: turn on a light, name a few things you can see, breathe slowly and remind yourself it was a dream.

Write the nightmare down, then write a new version in which the story changes in any way you choose, and go over the new version for a few minutes each day while awake (clinicians use a structured form of this called imagery rehearsal).
Talk about the dream with someone you trust; saying it out loud often loosens its hold.
Protect your sleep with regular hours and a calm wind-down, and avoid frightening media, alcohol and heavy meals late in the evening.
types.science: Levin and Nielsen (2007) proposed a model in which nightmares occur when the dreaming brain's normal work of calming fear memories is overwhelmed, a process influenced both by recent stress and by a person's general tendency to react to emotions with distress. Revonsuo (2000) suggested that threatening dreams may have evolved as simulations of danger. Imagery rehearsal, in which a person rewrites a nightmare and practises the new version, was tested in a randomised trial by Krakow and colleagues (2001), and a 2018 position paper of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (Morgenthaler and colleagues) supports its use. The Academy's International Classification of Sleep Disorders, third edition (2014), describes nightmare disorder for cases in which distressing nightmares are frequent and affect sleep or daily life; only a clinician can assess that.

lenses.freud: Freud first understood nightmares as wishes whose disguise had failed, so that the dream turned into anxiety. Later, struck by the repeated nightmares of soldiers after the First World War, he wrote in Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920) that some dreams return to a frightening event in an attempt to master it, an exception to his theory of wish fulfilment.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading often meets the shadow in nightmares: the pursuer or the monster may embody qualities, impulses or feelings you have disowned. In Jung's view the unconscious tends to mirror the attitude we take toward it, so turning to face such a figure, in the dream or in reflection, can change it.
lenses.hvdc: The coding would typically show high apprehension and other negative emotions, aggression with the dreamer as the victim, misfortunes (sometimes bodily ones), and frequent strangers, creatures or threatening figures. Researchers look for a cluster of these features across many dreams, rather than reading too much into any single frightening night.
lenses.modern: Modern research links nightmares to stress and to how the brain processes fear during REM sleep. Most nightmares are not replays of real events but images built from current emotions. Rewriting the dream while awake, improving sleep routines and reducing stress help many people, and specialists in sleep and trauma can offer more structured support.

types.caution: Nightmares now and then are normal. If they come often, disturb your sleep, make you dread going to bed, or affect how you feel during the day for weeks, talk to a doctor or therapist. Frequent nightmares are recognised in sleep medicine, and they can be helped, especially after a frightening or painful experience.

types.name: Sexual/Intimate
types.short: A dream of desire, attraction, closeness or intimacy, sometimes with people you would never expect.
types.description:
Sexual and intimate dreams range from a charged glance or a lingering embrace to clearly romantic or erotic scenes. They are a normal part of dreaming for adults of every age, gender and orientation, and they can feel pleasant, confusing, embarrassing or all three at once.

The partner in the dream is often a surprise: a colleague, an ex, a celebrity, a stranger, or someone you feel no attraction to while awake. This rarely means what it seems. Intimate dreams usually speak the language of closeness, so the person may stand for a quality you admire, a part of yourself you are getting to know, or a kind of connection you are seeking, rather than a literal wish.

Dreams of a partner being unfaithful, or of being unfaithful yourself, are also common, and they are usually about feeling insecure, overlooked or torn rather than about wanting to act. As always in DREAM CODE, the feeling is the best guide: desire, tenderness, guilt, longing, safety or unease can each point somewhere different.
signs: The dream centred on attraction, romance, physical closeness or desire.
You woke with strong feelings of pleasure, longing, embarrassment or confusion.
The dream involved someone unexpected, or someone from your past.
The emotional tone of intimacy (being wanted, safe or close) stood out more than the details.
types.may_reflect: Intimate dreams may reflect desire and sexuality in a straightforward way, but they often reflect wider needs as well: to feel close, seen and valued, to take on a quality the dream partner represents, or to work through a relationship that is changing. They can also mirror creative energy, confidence or vitality returning.
practices: Note the feeling first, then the person: what quality do you associate with them, and where might you want more of that quality in your life?
If the dream involved a current partner, ask whether it reflects a need for more closeness, attention or play, and consider sharing that need, not necessarily the dream.
If the dream left you feeling guilty, remember that dreams are not choices; reflect gently on what tension it might be showing you.
Keep these entries private if you prefer; your journal is yours, and nothing in it is shared unless you choose to share it.
types.science: Hall and Van de Castle's (1966) coding system treats sexual interactions as a separate class alongside aggression and friendliness, and in their norms such interactions appear in only a small share of dream reports. Later diary research, including work by Michael Schredl and colleagues, suggests that sexual dreams are reported by people of all genders and relate to waking attitudes and experiences, in line with the continuity hypothesis (Domhoff 2003). REM sleep brings physical arousal whatever the dream is about, which helps explain why intimate dreams can arise without any obvious waking cause.

lenses.freud: Freud placed desire at the heart of his theory and argued that many dreams carry sexual wishes in disguised form. With openly intimate dreams, a Freudian reading would still look past the obvious: who the partner might really stand for, what was forbidden or allowed, and which feelings from earlier relationships might be returning.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading often sees intimacy in dreams as a meeting with the anima or animus, in Jung's terms the inner figure of the other side of the psyche, or more broadly as a union of opposites. Joining with a dream partner can symbolise integrating the qualities that partner carries, a step toward wholeness rather than a literal desire.
lenses.hvdc: The coding records sexual interactions on a scale of intensity, together with the characters involved: known or unknown people, current or former partners. Across a dream series, the balance of sexual, friendly and aggressive interactions can say something about how you picture closeness and relationships.
lenses.modern: Modern research treats intimate dreams as continuous with waking life: they draw on current relationships, attractions, memories and media, and on the body's own arousal during REM sleep. They are better read as emotional statements than as literal plans or hidden verdicts about who you are.

types.caution: If intimate dreams bring back a painful or unwanted experience, or leave you distressed for days, consider talking with a therapist. You deserve support, and dreams like these can ease with care.

types.name: Grief/Loss
types.short: A dream that carries a loss: a person, a relationship, a home, a time of life or a version of yourself.
types.description:
Grief dreams carry the weight of loss. They may feature someone who has died, a relationship that has ended, a home you have left, a pet, a job, your health, or a time of life that has passed. Sometimes the loss is explicit: a funeral, a goodbye, an empty room. Sometimes it is only a feeling of searching, missing or sorrow that lingers after you wake.

After a death, many people dream of the person who died. Early dreams can be painful: the person is ill again, or you keep losing them, or you know in the dream that they are gone. Over time the dreams often change, becoming calmer, warmer or simply more ordinary. Some people find these dreams deeply comforting and others find them hard. Both are normal, and so is having no such dreams at all.

Grief dreams are part of how the mind absorbs a loss, revisiting the bond, the absence and the questions that remain. They keep no timetable, and a dream of loss can return years later, around an anniversary or a new change, as part of grief's natural rhythm.
signs: The dream centred on someone or something you have lost.
You felt sadness, longing or a sense of searching, in the dream or on waking.
The dream included a goodbye, a funeral, an empty place or an unfinished conversation.
You woke with a mixture of pain and closeness.
types.may_reflect: Grief dreams may reflect the ongoing work of mourning: missing someone, wishing for one more conversation, guilt or relief, or the slow adjustment to a changed life. They can also reflect losses that have nothing to do with death, such as a move, a breakup, a child growing up or a change in health. How the dreams change over time often mirrors how the grief itself is changing.
practices: Write the dream down, including what you wanted to say or ask; some people go on to write a letter to the person, or to what they have lost.
Notice how the dreams change over weeks and months; your journal can show you a path that is hard to see from day to day.
Share the dream with someone who also knew the person, or with a friend who will simply listen.
If it feels right, make room for a small act of remembrance, such as a walk, a photograph, a meal or a song.
types.science: Deirdre Barrett (1992) gathered dreams of the dead and described recurring patterns, from dreams in which the person seems alive and well to dreams of saying goodbye. Rosalind Cartwright's research with people going through divorce, described in The Twenty-four Hour Mind (2010), suggested that dreams which actively work over a painful loss are linked with better adjustment over time. Walker and van der Helm (2009) proposed that REM sleep reprocesses emotional memories so that they hurt less, and continuity research (Domhoff 2003) predicts that what matters most to us, including the people we love, keeps appearing in our dreams.

lenses.freud: In Mourning and Melancholia (1917), Freud described grief as the slow work of withdrawing attachment from someone who is gone. He also recorded dreams in which a dead person appears alive and unaware of having died, and read them as the wish that they were still here, held alongside the painful knowledge that they are not. A Freudian reading would attend to that tension.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading takes the figure of the lost person seriously, both as a memory of them and, on the subjective level, as the part of you they shaped or awakened. Grief dreams may be inviting you to carry forward what that person meant to you, so that the relationship becomes part of who you are.
lenses.hvdc: The coding would note sadness as the emotion and, when someone who has died appears, would count them among the dead and imaginary characters, one of the indicators the system tracks. Across a series of dreams, changes in emotion and in friendliness toward the person can trace how grief is evolving.
lenses.modern: Modern research sees grief dreams as emotional memory processing: REM sleep revisits strong attachments and losses, possibly helping the mind fit them into a changed picture of life. Many bereaved people describe dreams of the person as meaningful and comforting, though some find them distressing, especially early on.

types.caution: Grief dreams are a natural part of mourning. If grief feels overwhelming for a long time, if distressing dreams keep you from sleeping, or if you are struggling to get through daily life, a grief counsellor, therapist or doctor can help. You do not have to carry it alone.

types.name: Comfort/Nostalgia
types.short: A soothing or nostalgic dream that wraps you in safety, warmth or a cherished past.
types.description:
Comfort dreams feel like a warm blanket. You may find yourself in a childhood home, at a grandparent's table, in a garden you loved, with old friends, or simply somewhere peaceful where everything is all right. Some are full of nostalgia, the bittersweet sense of a time that has passed; others are quietly reassuring, with someone telling you not to worry, or a feeling of being held.

These dreams often appear when life is demanding. When you are stressed, lonely, unwell or going through change, the dreaming mind can reach back to the places and people it associates with safety. That is not a step backwards: it can be a way of gathering strength from what has steadied you before.

Comfort dreams are worth savouring and remembering. Their details, a smell, a song, the feel of a room, are often clues to what gives you a sense of home now.
signs: You felt safe, calm, held or at home in the dream.
The dream took you back to a place, a person or a time from your past.
You woke with a sense of warmth, sometimes mixed with a gentle ache of missing something.
Nothing much needed to happen; the atmosphere was the point.
types.may_reflect: Comfort and nostalgia dreams may reflect a need for rest, safety or belonging, especially during stressful periods. They can also show what home means to you, and remind you of resources, relationships and parts of yourself you can still draw on. A touch of sadness alongside the comfort is natural, since nostalgia is both sweet and wistful.
practices: Write down the sensory details of the dream, then choose one you could bring into waking life, such as a recipe, a piece of music or a walk somewhere similar.
Ask what made the dream place feel safe, and where in your life now you find, or could build, that feeling.
If the dream featured someone you have lost touch with, consider reaching out to them.
Before sleep, spend a minute recalling the dream's setting as a calming image.
types.science: Research on nostalgia by Wildschut, Sedikides, Arndt and Routledge (2006) found that waking nostalgia is often triggered by low mood or loneliness, and that it tends to strengthen feelings of social connection and lift mood, which may help explain why comforting, nostalgic dreams appear in hard times. Hall and Van de Castle's (1966) coding shows that familiar settings and known characters, including family, are common in typical dreams. Nielsen and colleagues (2004) described a dream-lag effect, in which experiences resurface in dreams around a week later, a sign that dreaming draws on memory across very different spans of time, from yesterday to childhood.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see comfort dreams as a wish to return to an earlier, safer time, a gentle form of what Freud called regression. Rather than a weakness, this can be read as the mind seeking rest, and the particular memory it chooses is a useful starting point for free association.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading might recognise the Great Mother archetype, the nurturing and sheltering side of the psyche, in dreams of being held or fed. Comfort dreams can compensate for a waking life that is too harsh or too busy, restoring a sense of being supported from within.
lenses.hvdc: The coding would note familiar settings (often a home), family members and old friends, friendly interactions and happiness, with few misfortunes. A childhood home may be coded as a familiar setting, or as a distorted one when the place is recognisable but changed.
lenses.modern: Modern views see comfort dreams as part of emotion regulation: the brain may call up memories associated with safety to balance current stress. They also show how dreams blend recent concerns with much older memories that share the same emotional tone.

types.name: Recurring
types.short: A dream, or a theme, that returns again and again, sometimes for years.
types.description:
A recurring dream comes back: the same house, the same chase, the same exam, the same tidal wave, sometimes almost identical each time and sometimes the same theme in new clothes. Many people have a recurring dream that began in childhood or during a hard period, and some notice that it returns whenever life presses on the same sore spot.

Most recurring dreams are unpleasant, with themes of being chased, falling, being unprepared, losing teeth or being trapped, but not all of them. Some are peaceful places the mind keeps returning to, or familiar houses with rooms still left to explore. Their persistence is the point: they seem to keep circling something that has not yet been settled.

Recurring dreams often change when the situation behind them changes. People find that a dream stops, softens or ends differently once they have made a decision, faced a conflict or come to terms with a loss. Your journal is the ideal tool for seeing this: following a recurring dream over time is one of the clearest ways to watch yourself change.
signs: You have had this dream, or one very like it, before.
The setting, the threat or the plot feels familiar even when the details change.
It tends to return at similar times, such as during stress or around certain dates.
You recognise it within the dream, or right after waking: “this one again”.
types.may_reflect: Recurring dreams may reflect an unresolved concern, a feeling that has not been fully expressed, or a pattern that keeps repeating in waking life. They often come back during periods that echo an earlier difficulty. A change in the dream (a new ending, a different feeling, someone coming to help) can reflect a real change in how you are meeting that concern.
practices: Record each time it happens and tick Recurring; over time your journal will show when the dream returns and what was going on in your life each time.
Ask what the dream's situation has in common with your life when it appears: being chased, unprepared or trapped often matches a specific waking feeling.
Imagine a different ending while awake and rehearse it briefly before sleep; with distressing recurring dreams, this often makes them return less often.
Share the dream with someone you trust and ask what they hear in it; a fresh perspective can reveal what you have overlooked.
Notice and record any change, however small; changes are often the most meaningful part.
types.science: Antonio Zadra (1996) reviewed research on recurrent dreams and found that their content is mostly negative, often involves threat, and tends to appear during stressful periods. Brown and Donderi (1986) found that people whose recurrent dreams had stopped reported better wellbeing than people who were still having them, which suggests that the end of a recurring dream can reflect resolution. Long dream series studied by Hall, and later by Domhoff (2003), show striking consistency in a person's dream characters and concerns across many years, in line with the continuity hypothesis.

lenses.freud: In Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920), Freud described a compulsion to repeat: the mind returns again and again to something painful, as if trying to master it. A Freudian reading of a recurring dream would look for the unresolved wish or conflict that keeps bringing the dream back, and for the point in the dream where it always breaks off.
lenses.jung: Jung gave recurring dreams special importance, as a sign that the unconscious is pressing a message that consciousness has not yet understood. In Man and His Symbols (1964) he suggested that they may compensate for a lasting one-sidedness in a person's attitude, or go back to a moment that left a mark. A Jungian reading would ask what the dream is trying to balance, and would watch closely for any change in the series.
lenses.hvdc: The coding system becomes most useful across many dreams, and recurring dreams are where that pays off. Coding each occurrence lets you compare characters, emotions, misfortunes and settings over time; a shift from apprehension toward happiness, or from failure toward success, is a measurable sign that the dream is changing.
lenses.haudenosaunee: Published accounts of Haudenosaunee dream teachings, such as the Jesuit Relations and Anthony Wallace's study Dreams and the Wishes of the Soul (1958), describe dreams as the language of the soul, carrying its hidden wishes, which the Jesuit writers recorded as ondinnonk. They also describe dreams that go unanswered returning, often more insistently, until the wish is heard. Read through these ideas, a recurring dream is a message still waiting for a reply. The response they point to is to ask what the dream wants, to share it with someone you trust who might help you hear it, and to honour it with a small, safe act in waking life, then notice whether the dream changes.
lenses.modern: Modern research links recurring dreams to unresolved stress and to how the brain processes threat and emotion. Their tendency to fade or change when life changes fits the continuity hypothesis. Rescripting, imagining a new outcome while awake, is used in clinical work with recurring nightmares, which shows that these dreams can be influenced.

types.caution: If a recurring dream is a nightmare that disturbs your sleep or your days for weeks, or is tied to a frightening experience, talk to a doctor or therapist; recurring nightmares can be helped.

types.name: Progressive
types.short: A dream that continues or develops across nights, like chapters of an unfolding story.
types.description:
Progressive dreams pick up where an earlier dream left off. You return to the same city and know your way a little better; your relationship with a dream character deepens; the house you keep visiting reveals a new room; a journey moves forward from one night to the next. Where a recurring dream tends to repeat, a progressive dream develops.

Sometimes the continuation happens within a single night, as dreams in later REM periods build on earlier ones. Sometimes it unfolds over weeks, months or years, a series you only notice when you read your journal back. A progressive dream can also be a recurring dream that has started to move: the chase that, one night, turns around.

Because they move, progressive dreams are often read as a picture of inner development. Watching where the story goes, and what changes in you within it, can reveal a process of growth or adjustment that is hard to see in daily life.
signs: The dream continued a setting, character or storyline from an earlier dream.
You recognised the dream world and noticed it had changed or grown.
A situation that used to repeat began to move forward or end differently.
Reading your journal reveals a sequence, like chapters.
types.may_reflect: Progressive dreams may reflect an ongoing process in your life: learning, healing, a relationship developing, a decision taking shape or a long transition. Changes in the dream (gaining confidence, finding a way through, being joined by helpers) can mirror changes in how you are meeting that process.
practices: Give the dream world or storyline a name in your journal so you can find each chapter easily.
When you record a new chapter, note what has changed since the last one: the setting, your role, the feeling, how it ended.
Before sleep, recall where the last chapter ended and set a gentle intention to return; some people find this invites the next instalment.
Every few months, read the whole series together and write a short summary of the journey so far.
types.science: Rosalind Cartwright's work, summarised in The Twenty-four Hour Mind (2010), described how dreams across a single night can build on one another, with later dreams linking a current concern to older memories. Jung's analysis of a long dream series in Psychology and Alchemy (1944) treated a sequence of dreams as a developing whole rather than a set of separate events. Domhoff (2003) argued that dream series read together reveal patterns in a person's concerns that single dreams cannot, and that these patterns change when waking life changes.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading would treat each chapter as part of one extended dream-work, with the same hidden concern finding new disguises over time. Freud noted that dreams from the same night often deal with the same material, and a series can show a wish or conflict moving gradually closer to open expression.
lenses.jung: Jung placed great weight on dream series, believing that a sequence shows the direction of individuation, the gradual process of becoming whole, more clearly than any single dream. A Jungian reading would follow the recurring figures and symbols as they transform, and ask where the journey is heading.
lenses.hvdc: Across a series, the coding can track change: whether aggression gives way to friendliness, failure to success, unfamiliar settings to familiar ones, or apprehension to happiness. Shifts like these only mean something across many dreams, which is exactly what a progressive series provides.
lenses.modern: Modern research suggests that dreaming integrates new experience with older memory over days and weeks, so a storyline that develops across nights fits the way memory consolidation unfolds. Progressive dreams also fit the continuity hypothesis: as waking concerns develop, their dream versions develop too.

types.name: Fragmented
types.short: A dream remembered as disconnected scenes or pieces that jump without clear transitions.
types.description:
Fragmented dreams arrive in pieces. You remember a beach, then a classroom, then someone handing you a key, with no sense of how one led to the next. Scenes cut abruptly, people change identity halfway through, and the thread of the story keeps snapping. Sometimes only a single image survives, vivid but without context.

Some of this comes from how dreams are built, since dreams often shift scene suddenly, and some comes from how they are remembered. Dream memory is fragile: on waking, details fade fast, and what remains are the most emotional or striking moments. Dreams from lighter, non-REM sleep also tend to be shorter and more fragmentary, and broken sleep, stress, illness or alcohol can make dreams more disjointed.

Fragments are still worth recording. Even a single image, a feeling or a scrap of dialogue can be meaningful, and fragments from the same night often share a theme or an emotion that links them below the surface.
signs: You remember several scenes but not how they connected.
The setting, the people or the plot changed suddenly without explanation.
Only a single image or moment remains from the dream.
The dream felt chaotic or hard to put into words.
types.may_reflect: Fragmented dreams may reflect a busy or scattered period, many concerns competing for attention, or disrupted sleep. They can also simply reflect the way memory captures dreams: in snapshots. The emotion that runs through the pieces is often the best guide to what connects them.
practices: Write every fragment down, in any order, without trying to make a story; a list of images is fine.
Look for what the fragments share: an emotion, a colour, a type of place, or a person who appears in different forms.
Lie still on waking and gently ask yourself “what came before this?”; extra pieces often return.
If your dreams are often scattered, look at your sleep: regular hours and less alcohol in the evening can make dreams more continuous and easier to recall.
types.science: Hobson and McCarley's (1977) activation-synthesis model proposed that the dreaming brain stitches a story together from bursts of internally generated activity, which could explain abrupt shifts of scene. David Foulkes (1962) found that dream reports from non-REM sleep are generally shorter and less story-like than those from REM sleep. Fosse and colleagues (2003) found that dreams rarely replay whole episodes from waking life and instead combine fragments of memory, which helps explain why dream scenes can feel like a collage.

lenses.freud: For Freud, fragmentation is part of the dream-work: condensation fuses several thoughts into one image, displacement shifts emphasis onto minor details, and gaps hide what the inner censor would not allow. Secondary revision, the mind's effort to tidy a dream into a story, does not always succeed and can leave pieces behind. A Freudian reading would associate to each fragment separately.
lenses.jung: Jung described a typical dream as having a dramatic structure: a setting, a development, a climax and a resolution. A fragmented dream is missing parts of that arc, and a Jungian reading would treat each piece as an image complete in itself, amplifying it with personal and cultural associations rather than forcing a plot onto it.
lenses.hvdc: The coding counts each setting separately, so fragmented dreams often show several settings, some coded as questionable or ambiguous, and fewer completed interactions. Short reports give the system less to work with, which is why it draws its conclusions from many dreams rather than from one.
lenses.modern: Modern research suggests that dream content is assembled from fragments of memory rather than replayed whole, and that recall on waking is highly selective. Fragmented recall is common and normal; how much you remember depends on when and how you wake, as well as on interest and practice.

types.name: Epic/Adventure
types.short: A grand, adventurous dream of quests, journeys, battles or vast worlds.
types.description:
Epic dreams feel like films or myths. You cross oceans and mountains, explore strange cities, fight battles, escape great dangers, lead or rescue others, or discover powers you did not know you had. They are often long and richly detailed, with many scenes and characters, and you may wake feeling as though you have lived through a whole saga.

These dreams are more likely in the long REM periods of the early morning, and after days full of stimulation, stories or games. People who play immersive games or read a lot of fantasy sometimes notice their dream worlds borrowing those landscapes. For some people epic dreams are frequent; for others they are rare and memorable.

Behind the spectacle there is often a personal story. The quest, the challenge and the role you play (hero, guide, outsider, bystander) can echo something you are facing or reaching for. Epic dreams can be thrilling, exhausting or inspiring, and many dreamers find them a source of creative ideas.
signs: The dream was long, with many scenes, places or characters.
There was a quest, a journey, a battle or a great challenge to meet.
You played an important role: hero, leader, rescuer or explorer.
The world of the dream felt vast, cinematic or mythic.
types.may_reflect: Epic dreams may reflect a period of challenge, ambition or transition, a sense that something important is at stake. They can also reflect a strong imagination and a mind rich in stories. The role you play and how the quest goes may mirror how you see yourself meeting challenges right now.
practices: Write the dream as a story, give it a title, and note your role and what the quest was for.
Ask what the challenge in the dream resembles in your waking life, and what help or strength the dream gave you to meet it.
Draw a map or a picture of the dream world; images often bring back forgotten scenes.
If you are creative, use the dream as raw material for writing, art or game ideas.
types.science: REM periods lengthen across the night, and reports from late-night REM sleep tend to be longer and more story-like, so the early hours are when epic dreams are most likely. Revonsuo's (2000) threat simulation theory sees chases, battles and escapes as rehearsals of danger, and the social simulation theory of Revonsuo, Tuominen and Valli (2015) adds that dreams also rehearse alliances, rescue and cooperation. Jayne Gackenbach's research on people who play video games suggests that frequent gamers report more dreams in which they take control or fight back, a sign of how waking experience shapes dream worlds.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading would see in the epic dream an open wish to be powerful, admired and invulnerable. In his essay Creative Writers and Day-Dreaming (1908), Freud compared adventure stories, whose hero always comes through, to daydreams in which the self takes the starring role, and an epic dream can be read in the same way.
lenses.jung: Epic dreams are fertile ground for a Jungian reading. The hero's journey, the descent into the underworld, the fight with the dragon and the treasure hard to attain are archetypal motifs Jung found in myths and dreams alike. A Jungian reading would ask what the quest means for your individuation, and which figures act as guides, tricksters or shadows.
lenses.hvdc: A long epic dream gives the coding a great deal to count: many characters, settings and objects (often travel, regions and weapons), aggressive and friendly interactions, successes and failures. Because long reports naturally contain more of everything, the system uses ratios, such as aggressions per character, so that a saga can be compared fairly with a short dream.
lenses.modern: Modern views see epic dreams as the brain's simulation engine at full stretch, blending memories, media and imagination into rehearsals of challenge and cooperation. They also show the creativity of the dreaming mind, its ability to combine fragments of experience into new worlds.

types.name: Mundane/Everyday
types.short: A dream of ordinary life: work, chores, errands, conversations and familiar places.
types.description:
Mundane dreams are made of everyday life. You answer emails, cook dinner, do the shopping, talk with a colleague, drive a familiar route or tidy the house. Nothing dramatic happens, and on waking you might wonder why your mind bothered. Sometimes the dream is so realistic that you briefly mistake it for a memory: did that conversation actually happen?

Ordinary dreams are more common than the dreams people tell. Laboratory studies that woke sleepers throughout the night found that most dream reports are fairly realistic, with familiar people and settings, while the bizarre dreams are the ones we remember and retell. Mundane dreams are the everyday texture of dreaming.

They can still be meaningful. Small details often carry the emotion: the tension in a routine meeting, the satisfaction of a finished task, a colleague who was kinder than usual. Mundane dreams also show what is occupying your mind, and they may help you rehearse or digest the day.
signs: The dream took place in a familiar, realistic setting such as home, work or a shop.
You were doing ordinary things: working, cooking, driving, talking.
Nothing impossible happened, or only one small odd detail.
You briefly wondered whether it had really happened.
types.may_reflect: Mundane dreams may reflect what is taking up your attention: workload, routines, responsibilities, relationships at work or at home. Frequent work dreams can suggest that work is spilling into your rest. Look for the one detail that differs from real life, or for the feeling running under the routine; that is often where the meaning lies.
practices: Note the one detail that differed from real life; small departures are often the most telling.
If work dreams are frequent, try a clear end-of-day ritual, such as writing tomorrow's list and closing the laptop, to help your mind put work down.
Record the feeling underneath the routine: calm, bored, pressured, satisfied.
If you mistake a dream for a memory, gently check the facts before acting on it.
types.science: Hall and Van de Castle's (1966) norms show that dreams are often set in familiar places with known characters, and Domhoff (2003) reviewed laboratory studies showing that most dreams collected across the night are more realistic and ordinary than the dreams people report spontaneously. This is the basis of the continuity hypothesis: dreams largely reflect waking concerns, people and activities. Fosse and colleagues (2003) found that dreams seldom replay a whole real event; even a realistic dream is usually a new combination of familiar pieces.

lenses.freud: Freud took ordinary dreams seriously, because he believed day residue, the small and seemingly trivial impressions of the previous day, was the material dreams use to carry deeper thoughts. A Freudian reading would ask why this particular trivial detail was chosen, and what more important thought might have been displaced onto it.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading might see a mundane dream as a sign that your unconscious largely agrees with your conscious situation, or it might look for the small compensating detail. Jung suggested that when the conscious attitude is reasonably balanced, dreams often stay close to everyday life.
lenses.hvdc: This is where the coding system is on home ground: familiar settings, known characters such as colleagues and family, household and work objects, few misfortunes and mild emotions. Hall's cognitive theory treats such dreams as plain statements of how you see your daily world, your roles and your relationships.
lenses.modern: Modern research treats mundane dreams as the clearest evidence of continuity between waking and dreaming. Going over routines and conversations in sleep may also help consolidate memories and prepare for the day ahead.

types.name: Prophetic/Precognitive
types.short: A dream that seems, looking back, to have anticipated something that later happened.
types.description:
Some dreams feel uncanny afterwards. You dream of someone you have not thought about in years and they call the next day, or a dream scene seems to match an event that happens later. People in every culture and era have reported dreams like these, and many describe them as among the most striking experiences of their lives. The feeling of recognition can be powerful, and sometimes unsettling.

Interest in such dreams is ancient. Dream books from antiquity, such as the Interpretation of Dreams written by Artemidorus in the second century, sorted the dreams thought to foretell events, and scriptures and histories record dreams that were taken as omens. In the twentieth century, the engineer J. W. Dunne's An Experiment with Time (1927) encouraged readers to write down their dreams and compare them with later events, something many people who keep a dream journal still try.

Science offers several ways to understand these experiences without dismissing them. With so many people dreaming every night, some dreams will match later events by coincidence. Memory favours the hits and forgets the misses, and a remembered dream can be quietly reshaped by what happens next. And the brain is a prediction machine: a dream can pick up on patterns, worries and cues you have not consciously put together, so it can be insightful about likely outcomes without seeing the future. DREAM CODE does not treat dreams as predictions; it invites you to explore what a dream that felt prophetic means to you.
signs: After an event, you felt you had dreamed it, or something very like it, beforehand.
The dream felt unusually clear, significant or different in quality from your other dreams.
You woke with a strong sense that the dream was about the future.
Details of the dream seemed to match something that happened later.
types.may_reflect: Dreams that feel prophetic may reflect your mind's sensitivity to patterns: signs in a relationship, a situation or your own body that you have noticed but not yet put into words. They can also reflect worry or hope about the future, rehearsed in images. Exploring what the dream drew on, and what you already sensed, is often more illuminating than asking whether it came true.
practices: Write the dream down with the date and time before anything happens, so you have an accurate record rather than a memory reshaped by events.
Record the dreams that do not match later events too; an honest record shows the whole picture.
Ask what you already knew or sensed that the dream might be drawing on.
If a dream seems to warn of harm, use it as a prompt for calm, sensible action, such as checking in with someone or booking a routine check-up, rather than as a certainty.
types.science: The statisticians Diaconis and Mosteller (1989) showed how the law of truly large numbers makes striking coincidences inevitable across a large population, which applies to dreams that seem to match later events. Research on memory since Bartlett's Remembering (1932) shows that recollection is reconstructive, and people tend to remember the matches and forget the many dreams that came to nothing. Hobson and Friston (2012) described the dreaming brain as continually generating and refining a predictive model of the world, which suggests how dreams can anticipate likely outcomes from known patterns. Controlled research has not established that dreams can foresee future events.

lenses.freud: Freud closed The Interpretation of Dreams by arguing that dreams come from the past, even though, by picturing a wish as fulfilled, they seem to lead into the future. In a short paper on a premonitory dream that appeared to come true, he argued that the sense of prediction had been built after the event. A Freudian reading would look for the wish or fear behind the dream.
lenses.jung: Jung distinguished the prospective function of dreams, their way of sketching possible developments from what the unconscious already perceives, from prophecy. He also wrote about synchronicity (1952), meaningful coincidences between inner and outer events, without claiming that one causes the other. A Jungian reading would explore what the coincidence means to you.
lenses.hvdc: The coding system describes what is in a dream, not whether it matched later events, so a prophetic dream would be coded like any other. Its content (characters, emotions, misfortunes) can still show which concerns were active at the time you dreamed it.
lenses.haudenosaunee: The published accounts of Haudenosaunee dream teachings, such as the Jesuit Relations and Anthony Wallace's 1958 study, describe a tradition that took dreams very seriously, with the emphasis, as Wallace presents it, on the soul's wishes rather than on forecasting. The Jesuit writers recorded dreams of misfortune being answered with a symbolic enactment in waking life, so that the dream was honoured without the misfortune coming to pass. Read through these ideas, the question a dream like this raises is less “will this happen?” than “what is this dream asking me to attend to now?”, and the answer might be a small, safe act that honours it.
lenses.modern: Modern research explains most precognitive experiences through coincidence, memory bias and the brain's predictive processing, which constantly forecasts what is likely to happen. A dream can draw on subtle cues, such as a change in someone's behaviour or in your own body, that you have not consciously registered, which can make it feel prophetic while it expresses what you already sensed.

types.caution: If a dream about harm, illness or death keeps worrying you, talk it over with someone you trust. If it concerns your health, a doctor can check what is bothering you; a dream is not medical information. If worry about dreams like this is affecting your sleep or daily life, a therapist can help.

types.name: Healing/Therapeutic
types.short: A dream that soothes, resolves or restores, leaving you lighter, clearer or more whole.
types.description:
Healing dreams leave you better than they found you. A conflict is resolved, an apology is given or received, a wound closes, a frightening figure turns gentle, someone takes care of you, or you simply wake with a sense of peace after a long struggle. Some are quiet and tender; others are dramatic turning points in a run of difficult dreams.

People have long looked to dreams for healing. In ancient Greece, people who were ill would sleep in sanctuaries dedicated to Asclepius in the hope of a dream that would bring relief or guidance, a practice known as incubation. Today, dream researchers and therapists describe how dreams can help process emotion, and how a dream that turns a painful story in a new direction can mark real emotional change.

A healing dream is not a cure and does not replace care, but it can be a meaningful sign of change and a source of strength to come back to. Recording it, together with the feeling it left, keeps that resource within reach.
signs: You woke feeling relieved, lighter, comforted or at peace.
A long-standing conflict, fear or sorrow resolved or softened in the dream.
You were cared for, healed or forgiven, or you cared for or healed someone else.
A dream that used to be distressing changed for the better.
types.may_reflect: Healing dreams may reflect emotional processing that is moving forward: grief easing, a conflict being accepted, a fear losing its grip, or self-compassion growing. They can also come as a kind of encouragement during recovery or transition. The particular image of healing (water, light, an embrace, a doctor, colour returning) can become a personal symbol worth remembering.
practices: Record the dream in detail, especially the moment of change and how your body felt.
Choose an image from the dream to come back to in moments of stress, as a short visualisation.
Ask what the dream suggests you need more of, such as rest, forgiveness, connection or care, and take one small step toward it.
If the dream relates to an ongoing difficulty, consider sharing it with a therapist, counsellor or trusted friend.
types.science: Walker and van der Helm (2009) proposed that REM sleep works as a kind of overnight therapy, reprocessing emotional memories in a brain state low in stress chemistry so that their emotional charge is reduced. Ernest Hartmann, in Dreams and Nightmares (1998), argued that dreams place emotion in context by making broad connections in a safe space, and described how dreams after trauma gradually change as the experience is integrated. Rosalind Cartwright's studies, summarised in The Twenty-four Hour Mind (2010), linked dreams that actively work through a painful situation with better recovery.
