lenses.freud: For Freud, the healing power of dreams lay in interpretation: bringing the hidden wish or conflict into awareness loosens its hold. A Freudian reading of a healing dream might see a wish for repair or reconciliation openly fulfilled, and would ask what the dream allowed that waking life does not yet allow.
lenses.jung: Jung saw the psyche as self-regulating and dreams as part of its healing work, compensating for imbalance and guiding the process of individuation. A healing dream may be the Self, the centre of wholeness, making itself felt, often through images of light, water, a wise figure or a reconciled pair.
lenses.hvdc: The coding would note friendly interactions, good fortunes, successes and happiness, sometimes in clear contrast with earlier dreams in a series. Hall's approach would read the change in these indicators over time as a shift in how you see yourself and others.
lenses.haudenosaunee: In the published accounts of Haudenosaunee dream teachings, notably Anthony Wallace's 1958 study, a person's wellbeing was closely tied to whether the soul's hidden wishes, its ondinnonk, were heard and answered, and the body was understood to take part in dreams. Honouring a dream through action in waking life was part of caring for the whole person. Read through these ideas, a healing dream is one in which a need of the soul is met or clearly shown; the response is to carry it into waking life in a small, concrete way, and perhaps to share it with someone you trust.
lenses.modern: Modern research supports the idea that sleep and dreaming help regulate emotion, with REM sleep linked to softening the emotional impact of memories. Clinicians use dream rescripting with recurring nightmares, which shows that changing a dream's story can change how a person feels.

types.name: Problem-Solving
types.short: A dream that offers an answer, an idea or a new angle on a problem you have been facing.
types.description:
Sometimes you go to sleep with a problem and wake up with an answer. A problem-solving dream might show you the missing piece of a design, a line for a story, a melody, a way to handle a difficult conversation, or simply a new way of seeing something. The solution can be literal, appearing exactly as you need it, or symbolic, arriving as an image you have to translate.

History is full of reported examples. The pharmacologist Otto Loewi said that the design of his Nobel Prize-winning experiment on chemical nerve transmission came to him in a dream; Paul McCartney has said that the melody of “Yesterday” arrived in his sleep; and the chemist August Kekulé told of a reverie in which a snake seized its own tail, suggesting the ring shape of benzene, though historians debate his account. Most problem-solving dreams are humbler, but just as useful.

This kind of dream can also be invited. Focusing on a problem before sleep, a practice known as dream incubation, seems to make related dreams more likely, although the solutions often need waking work to complete.
signs: You woke with an idea, answer or solution you did not have before.
The dream dealt, directly or symbolically, with a problem you were working on.
A dream image made sudden sense when you thought about your problem.
You felt a sense of clarity or discovery on waking.
types.may_reflect: Problem-solving dreams may reflect a mind that keeps working on what matters to you while you sleep, reorganising information and loosening rigid ways of thinking. They often come after a period of effort and frustration, when the waking mind has done the groundwork and needs a different angle.
practices: Before sleep, write your problem in one or two clear sentences and picture it briefly; this is the heart of dream incubation.
Keep this journal or a notebook close and record whatever you remember on waking, even if it seems unrelated.
Look for symbolic answers: ask how a dream image might apply to your problem.
Test dream ideas in waking life; the dream offers a lead, and waking judgement does the checking.
types.science: Deirdre Barrett (1993) asked students to incubate dreams about a personal or academic problem over a week and found that many dreamed about their problem, and that some felt a dream had offered a solution; her book The Committee of Sleep (2001) gathers examples from art, science and sport. Wagner and colleagues (2004) found that people who slept after working on a task were more likely to discover a hidden shortcut in it than people who stayed awake, suggesting that sleep can foster insight. Lacaux and colleagues (2021) found a similar effect for the lightest stage of sleep, just after falling asleep.

lenses.freud: Freud argued that the dream-work itself does not think or calculate; it only transforms. Any intellectual work in a dream, he held, comes from thoughts already present in waking life. A Freudian reading would therefore credit the solution to the latent dream thoughts, and ask which wish, perhaps to succeed or to be recognised, gave the problem its urgency.
lenses.jung: Jung believed the unconscious often knows more than the conscious mind and can offer solutions or new directions, part of what he called the prospective function of dreams. A Jungian reading would take the dream's answer seriously, especially when it comes through an unexpected figure such as a wise old man or woman, or a child.
lenses.hvdc: The coding would note successes by the dreamer and, often, objects such as tools, books, writing materials and devices. Hall's cognitive theory sees dreams as expressions of how we conceive of our problems and of ourselves, so a dream in which you succeed may reflect growing confidence as much as a technical answer.
lenses.modern: Modern research suggests that sleep helps restructure memories, find hidden patterns and connect distant ideas, which may explain sudden insights after sleep. REM sleep in particular has been linked to associative, creative thinking. Dream incubation is a practical way to aim this process at a question you care about.

types.name: Visitation
types.short: A dream in which someone who has died, or a guiding presence, seems to come and be with you.
types.description:
In a visitation dream, someone who has died seems to come to you. Often the dream feels different from ordinary dreams: clearer, calmer, more real. The person may look healthy and at peace, say a few words or nothing at all, offer reassurance, give you a hug, or simply be there for a moment before the dream ends. Some people describe similar dreams of a guiding figure, an ancestor, or a presence they cannot name.

Many bereaved people have dreams like this, and they often treasure them. A visitation dream can bring comfort, a sense of continuing connection, a chance to say goodbye, or a feeling that the person is all right. For some, it is an encounter with someone truly present; for others, it is the mind and heart bringing back someone deeply loved. DREAM CODE does not decide between these understandings; what matters is what the dream means to you.

Not every visitation dream is peaceful, and that is normal too. Some leave sadness, longing or unanswered questions. You may also never have one, and that says nothing about the depth of your love or your grief.
signs: Someone who has died appeared, often looking well and at peace.
The dream felt unusually vivid, real or different from your usual dreams.
A message, a reassurance or a simple presence seemed to be the point.
You woke with a strong feeling of having been with them.
types.may_reflect: Visitation dreams may reflect the continuing bond with someone you love, a need for reassurance or for closure, or a stage of grief in which the relationship is finding a new place in your life. They often come around anniversaries, important events or times of change. Whatever your beliefs, the feelings and words in the dream are worth holding on to.
practices: Write the dream down as soon as you can, especially any words spoken and how the person looked; details fade quickly.
Reflect on what you felt in their presence, and what that feeling might be offering you now.
If it feels right, share the dream with others who loved the person; dreams like this can be a gift to a whole family.
Honour the person in a small way that fits your life and beliefs, such as visiting a place they loved, cooking their recipe or doing something kind in their name.
types.science: Deirdre Barrett (1992) described common patterns in dreams of the dead, including dreams in which the person appears healthy and reassuring and dreams that seem to carry a message. Kerr and colleagues (2014), studying hospice patients near the end of life, found that many reported dreams and visions of loved ones who had died, most often experienced as comforting. The bereavement research gathered in Continuing Bonds by Klass, Silverman and Nickman (1996) describes ongoing bonds with those who have died as a common and often healthy part of grief, and dreams are one of the ways such bonds are felt. Science cannot settle questions about what lies beyond death; it can describe how these dreams are experienced and what they mean to people.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading would see the visitation dream as a wish fulfilled, the wish to see the person again, together with the work of mourning Freud described in Mourning and Melancholia (1917). Words spoken by the visitor might be read as words the dreamer longs to hear, or needs to say.
lenses.jung: Jung took dreams of the dead seriously as experiences of the psyche and did not reduce them to wishes. A Jungian reading would honour the figure both as the person themselves, as you carry them within you, and as a bearer of qualities, wisdom or guidance that you are now invited to carry forward.
lenses.hvdc: The coding would count the visitor among the dead and imaginary characters, one of the system's indicators, and would note friendly interactions and emotions such as happiness or sadness. Across your journal, how often these dreams come and how they feel can trace how your relationship with the person continues to change.
lenses.haudenosaunee: Published accounts of Haudenosaunee dream teachings, such as Anthony Wallace's 1958 study and the earlier Jesuit Relations, describe dreams as the language of the soul, never random. Through that idea, a dream in which someone who has died seems near would be listened to with care. The accounts speak of ondinnonk, the soul's hidden wishes, which can include longing or something left unsaid, and of honouring a dream through a small, real act in waking life. They also describe dreams being told to others so that people together could help hear what a dream asks; today that might simply mean sharing it with someone you trust.
lenses.modern: Modern research places visitation dreams within the continuing bonds that many bereaved people keep with those who have died. They often feel more vivid than ordinary dreams, and many people experience them as comforting. Researchers study how they are experienced and how they help, without claiming to settle what they ultimately are.

types.caution: Visitation dreams are usually comforting. If dreams of someone who has died are distressing, or grief feels overwhelming for a long time, talking with a grief counsellor, a therapist or someone you trust can help.

types.name: Archetypal/Mythological
types.short: A dream of mythic power, with universal figures, symbols or themes that feel larger than personal life.
types.description:
Archetypal dreams feel ancient. They may feature a wise old woman or man, a dark double, a trickster, a great mother, a divine child, a dragon guarding treasure, a journey into the underworld, death and rebirth, a flood, a sacred mountain or a labyrinth. The images often carry a strange weight and beauty, as if they belonged to a myth rather than to your own life.

Carl Jung called such figures archetypes: patterns he believed are shared by all humanity and appear in myths, religions, fairy tales and dreams everywhere. He also spoke of big dreams, dreams so striking that, as he noted on his travels, some communities treated them as belonging to everyone rather than to the dreamer alone. You do not need to accept Jung's theory to recognise the experience: some dreams feel as though they come from a deeper layer than everyday worries.

Archetypal dreams often appear at turning points: adolescence, love, parenthood, loss, illness, midlife or a change of path. Their imagery can be a way of seeing a personal moment as part of a larger human story.
signs: The dream featured mythic figures: gods, monsters, wise guides, tricksters or symbolic animals.
The setting or story felt timeless, like a myth, a fairy tale or a legend.
The images carried an unusual sense of power, awe, mystery or significance.
The dream stayed with you for days and felt important even if you could not explain why.
types.may_reflect: Archetypal dreams may reflect a significant life transition or a period of deep inner change. They can show qualities you are developing (courage, wisdom, nurture, cunning), conflicts you are working through, or parts of yourself that want recognition. Reading them as personal and universal at the same time can be rewarding.
practices: Identify the main figures and ask what quality each one represents, and where that quality appears, or is missing, in your life.
Explore myths, fairy tales or traditions that feature similar figures, then come back to your own associations.
Draw, paint or write about the central image; creative work often deepens the understanding of archetypal dreams.
Keep the dream in your journal and watch for related figures in later dreams; archetypal themes often recur across a series.
types.science: Jung's own introduction to archetypes for general readers is Man and His Symbols (1964). Archetypal theory is a framework for interpretation rather than a tested scientific model, and researchers continue to debate it. Harry Hunt, in The Multiplicity of Dreams (1989), described a family of intense dreams with mythic and aesthetic qualities, and Don Kuiken and colleagues have studied impactful dreams that leave strong emotional effects in waking life. Cross-cultural work such as Kelly Bulkeley's Dreaming in the World's Religions (2008) shows motifs recurring across traditions.

lenses.freud: Freud acknowledged that some dream symbols are widely shared, and late in his work he spoke of an archaic heritage. A Freudian reading would still look for the personal history behind the mythic image: a giant may be a parent seen through a child's eyes, and a quest may carry a family drama.
lenses.jung: This is the heart of Jungian dream work. A Jungian reading would amplify the images, setting them beside myths, fairy tales and religious symbols that share their themes, and ask what the archetype is bringing to consciousness. Jung saw such dreams as important moments in individuation, when the collective unconscious speaks.
lenses.hvdc: The coding would note creatures and imaginary characters, unfamiliar settings and, often, dramatic interactions and misfortunes. Archetypal dreams tend to stand out in a series because they depart from the familiar people and places that make up typical dream content.
lenses.modern: Modern research explains shared dream motifs through common human experiences, such as birth, family, danger, loss and the body, as well as shared cultural stories and media. Many researchers see archetypes as useful descriptions of these recurring patterns rather than inherited images. Either way, the emotional intensity of such dreams makes them memorable and personally significant.

types.name: Spiritual/Transcendent
types.short: A dream of awe, sacred presence, unity or meaning beyond the self.
types.description:
Spiritual and transcendent dreams carry a quality of the sacred. You may feel bathed in light, meet a holy figure, hear a voice of great kindness, sense unity with everything, see your life from above, or wake with a deep peace that lasts all day. For people of faith, such dreams may feel like contact with God, the divine or the sacred as their tradition understands it; for people without religious belief, they may feel like an encounter with beauty, meaning or connection that words cannot quite reach.

Dreams hold a central place in many of the world's religions and spiritual traditions, as channels of guidance, revelation, calling or blessing. Across cultures, people describe transcendent dreams that changed the direction of their lives, and such dreams are often remembered for years.

DREAM CODE respects every understanding of these experiences, religious, spiritual or secular, and does not decide what they ultimately are. It offers ways to reflect on what such a dream means to you and how it might shape the way you live.
signs: You felt awe, reverence, deep peace, love or a sense of unity.
The dream included light, sacred places, holy figures or a sense of divine presence.
You felt guided, called, blessed or given a message.
The dream felt more meaningful than ordinary dreams and stayed with you.
types.may_reflect: Spiritual dreams may reflect a search for meaning, a deepening faith, a period of questioning, a time of grief or transition, or a moment of inner integration. They often come at life's thresholds. What the dream asks of you, and how it might shape your values and actions, can matter more than explaining where it came from.
practices: Record the dream in full, including the feeling it left, which is often its most important part.
Reflect on it within your own tradition or worldview and, if you wish, share it with a spiritual mentor, a faith leader or a trusted friend.
Ask what the dream invites you to do, change or honour in waking life, and take one small step.
Return to the dream's central image in prayer, meditation or quiet reflection, as fits your beliefs.
types.science: Kelly Bulkeley's Dreaming in the World's Religions (2008) surveys the place of dreams across religious traditions. Harry Hunt, in The Multiplicity of Dreams (1989), described transcendent and mystical dreams as a distinct form of dreaming with strong aesthetic and emotional qualities, and Don Kuiken and colleagues have studied transcendent dreams among the impactful dreams that change how people feel after waking. Science can describe how such experiences feel and what they do for people; questions about the sacred lie beyond what it can test.

lenses.freud: Freud, who was not religious, discussed the feeling of oneness with the world in Civilization and Its Discontents (1930), calling it the oceanic feeling and tracing it to the earliest sense of being undivided from one's surroundings. A Freudian reading would explore personal associations to the sacred figures, for example with parents. This is one perspective among many, not a verdict on faith.
lenses.jung: Jung took religious experience seriously as a psychological reality and used the word numinous for an awe-filled encounter with something greater. A Jungian reading would see a transcendent dream as a meeting with the Self, the archetype of wholeness, and as an important moment in individuation, without deciding questions that lie beyond psychology.
lenses.hvdc: The coding system has no category for awe or reverence; such feelings would usually be coded as happiness, or occasionally as confusion. It would note settings such as places of worship or nature, and sometimes imaginary characters. This is a place where the coding captures only part of what the dreamer experiences.
lenses.haudenosaunee: Published accounts of Haudenosaunee dream teachings, including Anthony Wallace's 1958 study and the Jesuit Relations, describe dreams as the language of the soul, a view in which a dream that feels sacred is not a curiosity but something to be honoured. They describe dreams being acted on in waking life, and being told to others so that people together could help hear what the dream asked. Read through these ideas, the natural response to a transcendent dream is to let it shape something you actually do, and to share it with someone you trust, rather than only to analyse it from a distance.
lenses.modern: Modern research treats transcendent dreams as a distinct and intense form of dreaming that often has lasting effects on mood and outlook. It studies their emotional qualities and their place in people's lives, while leaving questions of ultimate meaning to each person's own beliefs.
